lede: An equation with a matrix in it is solved the way any equation is: undo whatever was done to the unknown. Adding and subtracting behave normally. Multiplying does not, because there is no dividing by a matrix, so the undo is the inverse — and it has to go in front on both sides.
can: Sort a matrix equation into the kind that needs subtraction and the kind that needs an inverse
Solve AX = B by writing X as the inverse of A multiplied by B, in that order
Clear an added matrix first, and say what shape the answer will be

text: Two kinds of equation, sorted first

md:
$A + X = B$ and $AX = B$ look alike and are not. The first is ordinary algebra: take $A$ from both sides, entry by entry, and $X$ is left.
The second cannot be done that way, because there is no dividing by a matrix. It needs the inverse. So the first thing to do with any matrix equation is decide which kind it is.

prompt: One tap to begin. Among the four equations in the card above, which one is solved simply by taking $A$ from both sides?
explain: $A$ is added to $X$, so subtracting $A$ undoes it. The two with $AX$ in them need the inverse, because $A$ is multiplying.

text: 1. When the matrix is added or subtracted

md:
Treat it exactly as you would a number equation. From $A + X = B$, take $A$ from both sides: $X = B - A$, worked entry by entry.
The direction matters. $X = B - A$, not $A - B$: every entry of the answer changes sign if you take them the wrong way round, and nothing in the layout will warn you.

prompt: For $A + X = B$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 3 & 5\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}9 & 1 \\ 0 & 8\end{pmatrix}$, the answer is $X = B - A$. What is the entry in row 1, column 1 of $X$?
explain: $9 - 4 = 5$. Taking them the other way round would give $-5$.

md:
From $AX = B$ there is nothing to divide by, so multiply instead — by $A^{-1}$, which is the matrix that undoes $A$.
Write the chain out. $A^{-1}AX = A^{-1}B$. The left side has $A^{-1}A$, which is the identity, and the identity leaves $X$ unchanged. So $X = A^{-1}B$.

title: Why an inverse and not a division
md: Division is defined for numbers because every number except zero has a reciprocal. Matrices have inverses instead, and only when the determinant is not zero. So "divide both sides by $A$" has no meaning; "multiply both sides by $A^{-1}$" has one, and it does the same job.

prompt: In the chain shown above, $A^{-1}AX = A^{-1}B$ becomes $X = A^{-1}B$. What happened to $A^{-1}A$?
options: It became the identity, which leaves $X$ unchanged
answer: It became the identity, which leaves $X$ unchanged
explain: An inverse multiplied by its own matrix is the identity, and the identity is the matrix version of $1$.

md:
The inverse goes **in front** of each side. That is called pre-multiplying, and it matters because $AB$ and $BA$ are different matrices.
Writing $A^{-1}$ in front on one side and behind on the other breaks the equation, and it is the slip the examiners look for here. One rule covers every question on this specification: inverse first, both sides.

title: Summer 2018, Unit 1, Question 5
md: This was really well done, and the candidates who saw that the inverse was the way in made good progress. The marks that went were mostly arithmetic slips, and now and then a product multiplied in the wrong order. Write $A^{-1}$ in front of both sides before you work anything out.

prompt: To solve $AX = B$, where should $A^{-1}$ be written?
options: In front of the left side only
explain: In front of $A$ so that $A^{-1}A$ becomes the identity, and in front of $B$ so the equation stays balanced.

text: 4. Know the shape before you start

md:
$X = A^{-1}B$, so the shape rule from matrix arithmetic decides what $X$ looks like. A $2 \times 2$ inverse multiplied by a $2 \times 1$ column gives a $2 \times 1$ column.
So if $B$ is a column, $X$ is a column, and an answer written as a square matrix is wrong before the arithmetic is read. Check the shape, then do the work.

prompt: $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix and $B$ is a $2 \times 1$ column. In the equation $AX = B$, what shape is $X$?
explain: $X = A^{-1}B$ is a $2 \times 2$ times a $2 \times 1$, so it is a column with two entries.

text: 5. When something is added as well

md:
$AX + C = B$ is both kinds at once, and the order is the ordinary one: clear the added matrix first, then deal with the multiplication.
Take $C$ from both sides to get $AX = B - C$, work out that column, and only then multiply by $A^{-1}$. Going straight to $A^{-1}B$ solves a different equation.

title: Matrix Equations part 1 - Corbettmaths
why: The same method worked through on several equations, with the inverse written in front each time.

prompt: For $AX + C = B$ with $C = \begin{pmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}11 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}$, the first step gives $AX = B - C$. What is the entry in row 1 of $B - C$?
explain: $11 - 3 = 8$. Only once $C$ is cleared does the inverse come in.

title: The other side, which CCEA does not set
md: An equation written $XA = B$ needs the inverse **after** $B$, as $X = BA^{-1}$. The Teacher Guidance for this statement excludes that form, so on this specification the inverse always goes in front. It is worth knowing the other case exists, and no more.

Sort a matrix equation before solving it: added, subtracted, or multiplying.
Solve $A + X = B$ as $X = B - A$, in that direction.
Solve $AX = B$ as $X = A^{-1}B$, with the inverse in front of both sides.
Clear an added matrix before you reach for the inverse.
Say what shape $X$ will be before doing any arithmetic.

A matrix equation is usually worth $4$ or $5$ marks, with the inverse found inside the same question, so the later marks ride on it. The marks go on the inverse, on the product set up with the inverse in front, and on the final entries. Stuck? Write the inverse in front of both sides and say which side each one is on: that line alone can earn a mark.
